pos: adj., n. (of the reforming monastic order founded at Cîteaux in 1098; a monk of that order)
etymology: From Latin Cistercium, the Latin name of Cîteaux in Burgundy.
biblical_def: The Cistercians were the reform party of western monasticism. In 1098 Robert of Molesme led twenty-one monks out of a comfortable Benedictine house into the marsh at Cîteaux, meaning to keep the Rule of Benedict literally rather than loosely, and above all to restore manual labour to men who had handed it to servants. They wore undyed wool, which is why Europe called them the white monks; they refused the tithes and manors that had made Cluny rich; they settled in waste places and drained, cleared and farmed them. Within Bernard of Clairvaux's lifetime the one house had become some three hundred and forty. This dictionary records them for what they recovered and for what no discipline could reach. They recovered labour, and Scripture dignifies it, “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10), and “In all labour there is profit” (Pro 14:23). They recovered plain worship against ornament. What they could not reach is the standing before God the order existed to secure, because that standing is not won by rule at all, “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28), and “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9). A reform of monasticism was still a reform inside a system that had put a ladder where God had put a gift.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Cistercian as a monk of the order of Cisteaux, a reformed branch of the Benedictines; an order as a religious fraternity under one rule; reform as amendment of what is corrupt; labour as bodily exertion for subsistence; and austerity as severity of life.
webster_full: CISTERCIAN, n. A monk of the order of Cisteaux, a reformed branch of the Benedictines, so called from the place of their origin in Burgundy.
ORDER, n. A religious fraternity or society of men, bound by certain rules and living under one discipline.
REFORM, n. A reformation; amendment of what is defective, vicious, corrupt or depraved.
LABOR, n. Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; particularly, the exertion of the limbs in occupations by which subsistence is obtained.
AUSTERITY, n. Severity of manners or life; rigor; strictness; harsh discipline.
scriptures: For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
corruption_summary: The reforming order of Cîteaux, 1098: labour and plain worship recovered, but justification still sought by rule rather than received by faith.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The modern misuse is sentimental rather than ideological: the white monks are made into a lifestyle brand, admired for simplicity and silence by readers who want the aesthetic without the obedience. The Cistercians themselves would have refused the compliment. They went into the marsh to work, and Scripture commends exactly that, “to work with your own hands, as we commanded you” (1Th 4:11).

The real correction runs the other way, and it is doctrinal. A reform that tightens a rule cannot mend what is wrong with rule-keeping as a ground of acceptance. Paul puts the whole weight elsewhere, “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Tit 3:5), and the measure of our best obedience is given plainly, “all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags” (Isa 64:6). The principle to recover is that austerity may discipline a body and can never clothe a soul.

pos: adj., n. (of the eremitical order founded by Bruno in 1084 at the Grande Chartreuse; a monk of that order)
etymology: From Latin Cartusia, the Latin name of the Chartreuse valley in Dauphiné.
biblical_def: The Carthusians are the strictest of the western orders and the one that never needed reforming, because it never relaxed. Bruno of Cologne settled six companions in the high valley of Chartreuse in 1084 and built not a dormitory but a row of separate cells around a cloister walk, each with its own garden and workbench. A Carthusian eats alone, works alone, prays most of the office alone, and joins the community only for night office, conventual mass and the Sunday meal. The order boasts, with some justice, that it was never reformed because never deformed. This dictionary records the Carthusians for the one thing they hold that Scripture plainly honours and for the error of making it a rule of life. Solitary prayer is commanded and exemplified, “when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door” (Mat 6:6), and the Lord himself sought it, “rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place” (Mar 1:35). But he sought it and returned. Scripture never makes withdrawal permanent, because it also forbids forsaking the assembly, “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25), and the first Christians did the opposite of a cell, “they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Carthusian as a monk of the order founded by Bruno, remarkable for austerity; a cell as a small close apartment of a monk; solitude as a lonely life; silence as forbearance of speech; and a recluse as one shut up from the world.
webster_full: CARTHUSIAN, n. One of an order of monks, so called from Chartreux, the place of their institution by Bruno, remarkable for their austerity.
CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison; also, a small cave or hollow place; the cave or hut of a hermit.
SOLITUDE, n. Loneliness; a state of being alone; a lonely life; forbearance of company.
SILENCE, n. Forbearance of speech in man; taciturnity; omission of speech.
RECLUSE, adj. Shut up; sequestered; retired from the world or from public notice; solitary.
scriptures: Mat 6:6
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Mar 1:35
And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: The eremitical order of the Grande Chartreuse, 1084: solitary prayer kept with unmatched rigour, and made permanent where Scripture makes it occasional.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that silence and solitude are instruments, not vocations. Scripture sets them in a rhythm with the assembly rather than against it: the Lord withdrew, “And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed” (Luk 5:16), and then came back to the crowds and the twelve. The closet is a place to go, not a place to live.

The live temptation the Carthusian cell represents is the quiet conviction that holiness grows in proportion to distance from other people. The New Testament arranges sanctification the other way, in company that files off the edges, “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17), and it treats absenting oneself from the gathering as a danger rather than an advance, “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25). A man may be very alone and very unsanctified.

pos: adj., n. (of the order of canons regular founded by Norbert of Xanten at Prémontré in 1120; a Norbertine)
etymology: From Latin Praemonstratum, the Latin name of Prémontré in Picardy.
biblical_def: The Premonstratensians, called Norbertines and in England the white canons, were founded by Norbert of Xanten at Prémontré in 1120. They were not monks but canons regular: clergy living under the Rule of Augustine in community, bound to the choir office like monks but ordained and sent out to preach and to serve parishes. The order spread through the Rhineland, the Low Countries, Bohemia, Hungary and England, and many of its houses still hold the parishes attached to them. This dictionary records the Norbertines because their mixed life sits closer to the New Testament pattern than enclosure does, and because the gap that remains is instructive. A pastor is supposed to be among people, teaching, “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15), and reading the text so the hearers understand it, “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense” (Neh 8:8). The office belongs to men whose households are visible, “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2). The white canons preached and kept celibacy, and so held one half of the apostolic pattern while a vow cut away the other, which Scripture never required, “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled” (Heb 13:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon as a dignitary of the church living under a rule; regular as subject to a rule; a preacher as one who discourses publicly on religion; a parish as the precinct committed to one minister; and a rule as a prescribed form of conduct.
webster_full: CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend or revenue allotted for the performance of divine service in a cathedral or collegiate church.
REGULAR, adj. Governed by rule or rules; instituted or initiated according to established forms or discipline.
PREACHER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one that inculcates any thing with earnestness.
PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.
RULE, n. A prescribed form or method of conduct; a maxim, canon or precept to be observed.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
corruption_summary: The order of canons regular of Prémontré, 1120: preaching clergy in community, apostolic in labour and unscriptural in the vow that forbade them wives.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that preaching is the work the ministry exists for, and that the man who does it is meant to be known and reachable. Nehemiah's platform is the model, where the text was read and then opened, “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). A canon in a parish is nearer to that than a monk behind a wall.

The live error is the vow that attached celibacy to office as a condition. Paul lists a wife among the qualifications rather than the disqualifications, “the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour” (1Ti 3:2), and names the apostles' own practice, “Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles” (1Co 9:5). Where a vow forbids what God calls honourable, the vow is the thing to repent of, “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” (1Ti 4:3).

pos: adj., n. (of the monastic family living under the Rule of Benedict; a black monk)
etymology: From Latin Benedictus, blessed, the name of Benedict of Nursia.
biblical_def: Benedictine describes every house living under the Rule that Benedict of Nursia wrote at Monte Cassino about 530, and so describes most of western monasticism before the twelfth century. The Rule is moderate by the standards of the Egyptian deserts: it fixes the hours of the office, divides the day between prayer, reading and manual work, requires stability so that a monk stays in the house he entered, and puts an abbot over him with wide discretion. Because it was moderate it was adopted everywhere, and because it was adopted everywhere it was relaxed everywhere, which is the whole explanation of Cluny, Cîteaux and every later reform. This dictionary records the Benedictines for a genuine debt and a genuine error. The debt is the copying of Scripture and the preservation of texts through centuries when nobody else was copying anything, work Paul himself valued, “bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13). The error is older than the Rule and survives every reform of it: the belief that this manner of life is a higher calling, when Scripture ranks no Christian above another, “for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8), and gives the whole church one priesthood, “ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9), and one mediator, “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Benedictine as a monk of the order of St Benedict; a rule as a prescribed method of conduct; an abbot as the governor of a monastery; stability as fixedness; and moderation as restraint of excess.
webster_full: BENEDICTINE, n. One of an order of monks, who profess to follow the rules of St Benedict; they are called black monks from the color of their habit.
RULE, n. A prescribed form or method of conduct; a maxim, canon or precept to be observed.
ABBOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
STABILITY, n. Steadiness; stableness; firmness; fixedness; the state of being established.
MODERATION, n. Restraint of violent passions or indulgence of appetite; equanimity; calmness of mind.
scriptures: The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.
Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
corruption_summary: The monastic family of the Rule of Benedict, c. 530: the copyists the West owes its books to, and the two-tier Christianity Scripture does not permit.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honest debt. Benedictine scriptoria kept the text of Scripture in circulation for a thousand years, and the apostle who sent for his parchments from prison would have understood the labour exactly, “bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13). A Protestant who despises the copyists is reading a Bible they handed him.

The error to name is the two-tier church. If the monk's life is a higher state, then the farmer's is a lower one, and the New Testament knows nothing of the arrangement. Christ forbids the title that ranks brother above brother, “But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ” (Mat 23:8); the whole body is priestly, “And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father” (Rev 1:6); and the perfecting is already done by one offering, not graded by a rule, “by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14).

pos: adj., n. (of the Benedictine congregation centred on Cluny from 910; a monk of that congregation)
etymology: From Cluny in Burgundy, with the adjectival ending -ac.
biblical_def: Cluniac describes the great Burgundian congregation founded in 910, which for two centuries was the most powerful religious body in Europe. Cluny's distinctives were freedom from local lords and bishops, a chain of dependent priories ruled from the mother house, and above all an immensely expanded liturgy. Where Benedict had balanced prayer, reading and manual work, Cluny filled the day with choir, lengthened the psalmody, built the largest church in Christendom, and handed the fields to servants and serfs. Its wealth and its abandoned spade are precisely what Cîteaux was founded to protest. This dictionary records Cluny because its history is a clean case study in a danger Scripture names directly. Worship can be multiplied until the multiplying becomes the point, and the Lord weighs such service by whether it was rendered to him at all, “did ye at all fast unto me, even to me?” (Zec 7:5). He prefers obedience to volume, “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams” (1Sa 15:22), and he rejects worship whose content is human invention, “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). The abandoned labour is its own rebuke, because work was commanded, “put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it” (Gen 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a priory as a convent subordinate to an abbey; liturgy as a form of prayers; psalmody as the practice of singing psalms; splendour as great brightness or magnificence; and wealth as large possessions.
webster_full: PRIORY, n. A convent of which a prior is the superior; in dignity below an abbey.
LITURGY, n. In a general sense, all public ceremonies that belong to divine service; a formulary of public devotions.
PSALMODY, n. The act, practice or art of singing sacred songs.
SPLENDOR, n. Great brightness; magnificence; pomp; parade; as the splendor of equipage or ceremonies.
WEALTH, n. Riches; large possessions of money, goods or land; that abundance of worldly estate which exceeds the estate of the greater part of the community.
scriptures: Zec 7:5
Speak unto all the people of the land, and to the priests, saying, When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month, even those seventy years, did ye at all fast unto me, even to me?
And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Gen 2:15
And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
corruption_summary: The Burgundian congregation of Cluny, 910: liturgy multiplied until worship became volume, and the spade handed to someone else.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that worship is measured by its object and its obedience, not by its length or its architecture. The prophet asks the question that undoes a swollen calendar, “did ye at all fast unto me, even to me?” (Zec 7:5), and Samuel sets the order of worth once for all, “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1Sa 15:22).

The second Cluniac error is quieter and far more common among Protestants: the assumption that holy work means work that is not manual. Scripture puts man in a garden to dig before there is any altar to tend, “put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it” (Gen 2:15), calls the hands' work worth establishing, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17), and leaves no room for a piety that needs a servant to feed it, “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10).

pos: n. (the monastic rule written by Benedict of Nursia about 530, governing most western monasteries for a thousand years)
etymology: From Latin Regula Benedicti, the rule of Benedict, from regula, a straight-edge.
biblical_def: The Rule of Benedict is seventy-three short chapters written at Monte Cassino about 530, and it is the most influential document in western monastic history. It appoints the hours of the office, apportions the day between prayer, reading and manual work, requires stability so that a monk remains in the house he entered, sets out the degrees of humility, regulates food, sleep, clothing, the reception of guests and the correction of faults, and grants the abbot wide discretion, charging him to temper the Rule to the weak. Its temper is the reason it conquered the West: it is severe enough to be a discipline and mild enough to be kept. This dictionary records the Rule for the goods it protects and the claim it cannot support. It protects reading, and Scripture requires a daily reading that shapes the reader, “he shall read therein all the days of his life” (Deu 17:19). It protects hospitality, which is commanded, “Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality” (Rom 12:13). It protects humility, “in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves” (Phi 2:3). What it cannot support is the weight laid upon it, because no rule added to Scripture may bind a conscience, “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rule as a prescribed form of conduct; a precept as a commandment intended as an authoritative rule; discipline as instruction and government; humility as lowliness of mind; and obedience as compliance with a command.
webster_full: RULE, n. A prescribed form or method of conduct; a maxim, canon or precept to be observed.
PRECEPT, n. Any commandment or order intended as an authoritative rule of action.
DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government, comprehending the communication of knowledge and the regulation of practice.
HUMILITY, n. In ethics, freedom from pride and arrogance; lowliness of mind; a modest estimate of one's own worth.
OBEDIENCE, n. Compliance with a command, prohibition or known law and rule of duty prescribed.
scriptures: And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:
Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.
Phi 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
corruption_summary: Benedict's seventy-three chapters, c. 530: daily reading, hospitality and humility protected, and a rule set beside Scripture where Scripture forbids additions.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Rule's best provisions are borrowed from Scripture and belong to every Christian household, not to monks. Daily reading is commanded of a king, “that he may learn to fear the LORD his God” (Deu 17:19); teaching through the ordinary hours of a day is commanded of a father, “when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way” (Deu 6:7). A family can keep more of the Rule than it imagines, and needs no vow to do it.

The error is the standing the Rule acquired. A document that regulates diet, sleep and clothing, and binds a conscience to them under vow, has crossed a line Scripture draws twice, “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32) and “Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee” (Pro 30:6). Paul names the regulating of food and touch as the very shape of a false discipline, “Touch not; taste not; handle not” (Col 2:21), and tells us plainly what such rules achieve, “not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23).

“not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23) — what regulation finally accomplishes.

pos: n. (c. 1028–1111, Burgundian abbot, founder of Molesme and first abbot of Cîteaux)
etymology: Robert, from Germanic hrod, fame, and beraht, bright; of Molesme in Burgundy.
biblical_def: Robert of Molesme was a Burgundian nobleman who became a monk, grew dissatisfied with the slackness he found, and spent his life founding houses and leaving them. He established Molesme about 1075; it prospered, filled with gifts and recruits, and relaxed in the prospering, which was the pattern he had fled. In 1098 he took twenty-one monks south to the waste ground at Cîteaux and became its first abbot. Within a year the monks of Molesme petitioned Rome, and Robert was ordered back to the house he had abandoned; he returned, governed it until his death in 1111, and left Cîteaux to Alberic and to Stephen Harding, who made it an order. This dictionary records Robert for a pattern worth seeing clearly. He discovered twice that prosperity dissolves discipline, which Scripture warns of in advance, “give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me” (Pro 30:8). He discovered also that a man may relocate without arriving, because the fault he kept meeting was not in Molesme, “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mat 26:41). The rest Scripture offers is not found at a new site but in a direction, “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16), and the contentment he never located is a thing learned, “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content” (Phi 4:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a founder as one who establishes or endows; an abbot as the governor of a monastery; prosperity as successful progress; discontent as uneasiness of mind; and content as rest or quietness of mind in the present condition.
webster_full: FOUNDER, n. One that founds, establishes and erects; one that begins, or lays a foundation; one from whom any thing originates.
ABBOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
PROSPERITY, n. Advance or gain in any thing good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise; attainment of the object desired.
DISCONTENT, n. Want of content; uneasiness or inquietude of mind; dissatisfaction at any present state of things.
CONTENT, n. Rest or quietness of the mind in the present condition; satisfaction which holds the mind in peace.
scriptures: Pro 30:8
Remove far from me vanity and lies: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me:
Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Phi 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
corruption_summary: Burgundian abbot, c. 1028–1111: founded Molesme, founded Cîteaux, was recalled to the first, and proved that a man may move without mending.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that prosperity is a harder test than hardship, and that Robert failed it twice without ever being an unserious man. Agur asks for the middle portion precisely because both ends are dangerous, “give me neither poverty nor riches” (Pro 30:8), and the Lord warns that a life is not measured by its holdings at all, “a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15).

The live temptation in Robert's story is the one every restless Christian knows: the conviction that the next place will be the faithful one. He founded, left, founded, and was sent back. Scripture offers rest along the old way rather than at a new address, “ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16), and it treats contentment as something acquired in whatever place a man already stands, “in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content” (Phi 4:11). Relocation is not repentance.

pos: n. (d. 1134, Englishman, third abbot of Cîteaux, author of the Charter of Charity)
etymology: Stephen, from Greek stephanos, a crown; Harding, an English patronymic.
biblical_def: Stephen Harding was born in Dorset, educated at Sherborne, travelled to Scotland and to Rome, and became a monk of Molesme before following Robert to Cîteaux in 1098. He became its third abbot about 1109, when the house was nearly extinct, and he governed it through the arrival in 1113 of a party of thirty Burgundians that included Bernard of Clairvaux. His lasting work is the Carta Caritatis, the Charter of Charity: a constitution binding every Cistercian house to the same usages, providing for annual visitation and a yearly general chapter at Cîteaux, and forbidding the mother house to tax its daughters. It is the first federal constitution in European religious history, and it is the reason the order held its shape while Cluny's chain of priories did not. Stephen also had the Latin Bible of Cîteaux corrected against Hebrew manuscripts, consulting Jews in order to get the text right. This dictionary records him for that textual conscience, which is recognisably biblical, “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15), “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8), and for constitutional charity, which answers a real need, “Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3), “whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a charter as a written instrument conferring rights; charity as love and good will; a constitution as the established form of government; visitation as the act of a superior who inspects; and a chapter as an assembly of ecclesiastics.
webster_full: CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man.
CHARITY, n. In a general sense, love, benevolence, good will; that disposition of heart which inclines men to think favorably of their fellow men, and to do them good.
CONSTITUTION, n. The established form of government in a state, kingdom or country; a system of fundamental rules and principles.

VISITATION, n. The act of visiting or state of being visited; the act of a superior or superintending officer, who visits a corporation or religious house to examine into the manner in which it is conducted.
CHAPTER, n. An assembly of the clergy of a cathedral or collegiate church, or of the members of a religious order.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
corruption_summary: English third abbot of Cîteaux, d. 1134: wrote the Charter of Charity, corrected the abbey's Bible against the Hebrew, and bound authority to service.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Stephen's textual conscience. He did not assume the Latin in front of him was right; he sought out men who could read the Hebrew and corrected the copy. That instinct is commanded, “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15), and it rests on what the text is, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16). A man who will not check his Bible against the original has less reverence for it, not more.

The second thing to recover is his constitutional restraint. The Charter forbade Cîteaux to live off its daughter houses, which is church government built on the apostolic warning against lordship, “Neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3), and on the Lord's inversion of greatness, “let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26). Stephen wrote a structure that assumed abbots would be tempted to dominate, and limited them in advance. That is wisdom any eldership can use.

pos: n. (c. 1030–1101, chancellor of Reims, founder of the Carthusian order)
etymology: Bruno, from Germanic brun, brown; of Cologne, his birthplace on the Rhine.
biblical_def: Bruno was born at Cologne, taught in the cathedral school at Reims for some twenty years, and rose to be chancellor of that archdiocese. He resigned and withdrew after a public quarrel with a simoniac archbishop, and in 1084 Bishop Hugh of Grenoble gave him the high valley of Chartreuse, where he and six companions built separate cells around a common cloister. Six years later Urban II, who had been his pupil, summoned him to Rome as an adviser; Bruno obeyed, found the curia unbearable, and was permitted to withdraw again, this time to La Torre in Calabria, where he died in 1101. He left no rule; the Carthusian customs were written down a generation later by Guigo. This dictionary records Bruno because his life turns on a decision Scripture treats with real sympathy and real limits. He fled a corrupt office, and a man may lawfully refuse to profit from corruption, “the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10). He sought silence, and the Lord sought it too, “he went up into a mountain apart to pray” (Mat 14:23). But the pattern he built made permanent what Scripture keeps occasional, and the standing he hoped to gain in the valley was never on offer there, “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law” (Phi 3:9), “For by grace are ye saved through faith” (Eph 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chancellor as a high judicial officer; to resign as to give up a claim or office; a desert as an uninhabited tract; silence as forbearance of speech; and renunciation as the act of disclaiming or rejecting.
webster_full: CHANCELLOR, n. A judge, or president of a court of chancery; in some churches, an officer who holds the bishop's court.
RESIGN, v.t. To give up; to yield; as, to resign a claim to a title or an estate; to withdraw from an office.
DESERT, n. An uninhabited tract of land; a region in its natural state; a wilderness; a solitude.
SILENCE, n. Forbearance of speech in man; taciturnity; omission of speech.
RENUNCIATION, n. The act of renouncing; a disclaiming or rejecting; as the renunciation of a title or a claim.
scriptures: For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
And when he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into a mountain apart to pray: and when the evening was come, he was there alone.
Phi 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
corruption_summary: Chancellor of Reims turned hermit, c. 1030–1101: founded the Grande Chartreuse, refused preferment twice, and sought in a valley what grace alone gives.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that refusing a corrupt office can be an act of obedience rather than of weakness. Bruno walked away from a see that was being bought and sold, and the apostolic warning he was heeding is blunt, “which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith” (1Ti 6:10). He was then summoned by a pope who had been his student, obeyed, and asked leave to go again. There is nothing pious about clinging to influence.

The error is in what the cell was expected to do. Bruno sought a place where the soul could be safe, and no such place exists on a map. Paul abandons the whole project of an owned righteousness, “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law” (Phi 3:9), and names the only ground there is, “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8). The Chartreuse valley is beautiful and silent and cannot justify a man.

pos: n. (c. 1080–1134, founder of the Premonstratensian canons and archbishop of Magdeburg)
etymology: Norbert, from Germanic nord, north, and beraht, bright; of Xanten on the lower Rhine.
biblical_def: Norbert was a Rhineland nobleman and a canon of Xanten who held benefices without serving them and lived at the courts of the archbishop of Cologne and the emperor. A brush with death in a thunderstorm turned him; he sold what he had, was ordained, and began preaching repentance so bluntly that his own chapter drove him out. He preached barefoot through northern France, and in 1120 Bishop Bartholomew of Laon gave him the wooded valley of Prémontré, where he gathered clergy under the Rule of Augustine into an order of canons regular who would both keep choir and preach. In 1126 he was made archbishop of Magdeburg and spent his remaining years reforming that see against violent resistance. This dictionary records Norbert for the shape of his conversion and the shape of his work. He had held office for its income and then repudiated it, which is the very sin Scripture names in a shepherd, “Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3). He became a preacher, and the preacher's trade is the priest's proper one, “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7). He gave away his estate, hearing the call literally, “go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor” (Mat 19:21), and found what Christ promised the obedient, “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Mat 6:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon as a dignitary of the church; a benefice as an ecclesiastical living; to preach as to pronounce a public discourse on sacred subjects; conversion as a change from one state to another, in theology a turning to God; and a reformer as one who effects amendment.
webster_full: CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend or revenue allotted for the performance of divine service in a cathedral or collegiate church.
BENEFICE, n. In the middle ages, an estate in land granted for life only; in church affairs, an ecclesiastical living.
PREACH, v.i. To pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject, or from a text of Scripture.
CONVERSION, n. In a theological or moral sense, a change of heart, or dispositions, in which the enmity of the heart to God is subdued, and is succeeded by love.
REFORMER, n. One who effects a reformation or amendment; one who labors to reform morals or manners.
scriptures: Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me.
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
corruption_summary: Rhineland pluralist turned barefoot preacher, c. 1080–1134: founded Prémontré, reformed Magdeburg, and gave away what he had once held for its income.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Norbert's besetting sin before his conversion is a live one still: holding a church office for its benefits while someone else does the work. Scripture puts the matter in terms no committee can soften, “Neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3), and fixes what the office is actually for, “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7).

His renunciation also needs its proper reading. The command to sell was given to one rich young man whose possessions were his god, and Norbert was in precisely that position, so he was right to take it as his own, “go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor” (Mat 19:21). What Scripture never does is make voluntary poverty a general law or a merit; the treasure is promised to the obedient, not purchased by the destitute, “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:20). The call is to loose a grip, not to acquire a rank.
